name: Containers and Orchestration
intent: Package an app with its dependencies into a container, then let an orchestrator keep the desired number of copies running, placed sensibly across machines, even when machines die.
scenario: A web deployment asks for 6 replicas on a 4-node cluster, each pod requesting 1000m CPU on 4000m nodes. The scheduler spreads the pods, then Node 2 dies. The controller sees 4 running against 6 desired and creates 2 replacements, which the scheduler places on the surviving nodes.
problem: Running software on hand-managed servers means every machine has slightly different libraries, copies get placed by whoever logged in last, and a dead machine means a page at 3 am. You need a repeatable package that runs the same everywhere, and something that continuously decides where copies run, notices when reality drifts from what you asked for, and fixes it without a human.

howItWorks.title: A container is a process with a private view of the host
howItWorks.text: A container is not a small VM. It is an ordinary process on the host kernel, isolated by namespaces (its own view of processes, network, mounts, hostname) and limited by cgroups (CPU shares, a memory ceiling). It starts in milliseconds and costs megabytes, but it shares the host kernel, so isolation is weaker than a VM with its own kernel.

howItWorks.title: An image is read-only layers; the container adds a thin writable one
howItWorks.text: An image is a stack of immutable layers, one per build step, identified by content hash. Layers are cached and shared, so ten services on the same base image store that base once. Put rarely changing steps (OS, dependencies) first and your code last, so a code change rebuilds and ships only the top layer.

howItWorks.title: You declare desired state; controllers reconcile it
howItWorks.text: You tell the API server what you want (a Deployment with 6 replicas of image web:2.4). It stores that. A controller runs a loop forever: observe actual state, compare with desired, act to close the gap (create or delete pods), repeat. Because it is level-triggered, a missed event or a crashed controller self-corrects on the next pass.

howItWorks.title: The scheduler filters nodes, then scores them
howItWorks.text: For each unplaced pod the scheduler first filters out nodes that cannot host it: not enough unreserved CPU or memory after the sum of existing pods' requests, wrong labels, taints, and so on. Among those that remain it scores: spreading prefers the emptiest node (resilience), bin-packing prefers the fullest that still fits (cost, and whole nodes left free to switch off). If no node passes the filter the pod stays Pending.

howItWorks.title: Requests reserve; limits cap
howItWorks.text: A request is what the scheduler reserves and what the pod is guaranteed under contention. A limit is a runtime ceiling enforced by the kernel: CPU above the limit is throttled, memory above the limit gets the container OOM-killed. Because only requests count when placing, the sum of limits on a node can exceed its capacity (overcommit). That is fine while load is modest and ends in OOM kills when many pods burst together.

howItWorks.title: Probes and node failure feed the same loop
howItWorks.text: A liveness probe failing makes the kubelet restart the container; a readiness probe failing removes the pod from the Service endpoints so no traffic reaches it. When a node stops reporting (about 40 s by default), its pods are marked lost and, after the eviction timeout, deleted. The controller then sees fewer pods than desired and creates replacements, which the scheduler places on healthy nodes.

pros: The same image runs on a laptop, in CI and in production, which removes most works-on-my-machine bugs
Self-healing: crashed containers restart and lost nodes are replaced automatically
Declarative desired state is reviewable, versionable and repeatable
Dense, cheap packing of many workloads on shared machines
Rolling updates, scaling and rollbacks are built-in operations, not scripts
cons: Significant operational complexity: networking, storage, RBAC, upgrades and a control plane to understand
Containers share a kernel, so a kernel exploit or noisy neighbour crosses the boundary in a way it does not with VMs
Stateful workloads (databases) are much harder than stateless ones
Misconfigured requests and limits cause either wasted money or surprise kills
A cluster that is sized wrongly or has too few nodes fails in surprising, capacity-shaped ways
whenToUse: Many services or many copies of a service that need consistent packaging and automated placement
Workloads that must survive a machine failing without someone being paged to restart them
Teams that deploy often and want rolling updates, rollbacks and autoscaling as standard operations
Anything you might move between clouds or between environments
whenNotToUse: A single small app on one server: a plain process manager or a managed platform is simpler
A team without the time to learn and operate a cluster, when a managed container service or PaaS would do
Workloads needing strong multi-tenant isolation from untrusted code, unless you add VM-level sandboxing
Latency-critical or hardware-bound jobs that need dedicated machines or specific kernel features
pitfalls: No resource requests: the scheduler thinks pods are free, packs far too many onto one node, and they fight for CPU
Memory limit set equal to a typical value: any burst is an OOM kill and a restart loop
Failure domains ignored: all replicas land on one node or one zone, so one failure takes the whole service down (use anti-affinity or topology spread)
Liveness probe that checks a dependency such as the database: when the database is slow every pod restarts at once and makes it worse
Readiness and liveness probes pointing at the same slow endpoint with a tight timeout, causing restart storms during load spikes
Replicas sized to exactly fill the cluster: after one node dies the replacements stay Pending because the survivors have no headroom
Using the latest tag or a mutable image tag, so two nodes run different code under the same name

roles.label: API server
roles.description: Stores desired state (the Deployment says 6 replicas) and the current pod list; everything else watches and updates it.

roles.label: Controller
roles.description: Runs the reconcile loop: compares desired and actual pods and creates or deletes pods to close the gap.

roles.label: Scheduler
roles.description: Picks a node for each unplaced pod by filtering on free CPU and memory (requests) and scoring by policy.

roles.label: Node
roles.description: A machine with a kubelet that runs the pods, runs probes and reports its health.

quiz.question: A Deployment asks for 5 replicas. The controller process crashes and stays down for 10 minutes. During that time 2 pods die. The controller restarts. What happens next?
options: It replays the missed pod-death events from a log before it creates the 2 pods.
The 2 pods stay down until an operator applies the Deployment again.
It compares 3 running pods with 5 desired and creates 2, without needing the events it missed.
It restarts all 5 pods to return to a known clean state.
quiz.explanation: Controllers are level-triggered: each pass compares the current state with the desired state and closes the gap, so missed events do not matter. Re-applying the manifest or restarting everything is not needed.

quiz.question: A cluster has 4 nodes, each with 4000m allocatable CPU. A Deployment runs 8 replicas, each requesting 2000m, so the cluster is exactly full. One node dies. What happens to the 2 pods it was running?
options: The replacements stay Pending because the survivors have no unreserved CPU left.
The replacements start on the survivors anyway and share CPU through throttling until a node returns.
The kubelet evicts two other pods so the replacements can fit.
The controller schedules them back onto the dead node until it returns.
quiz.explanation: The scheduler places pods by requests, and the three surviving nodes are already fully reserved, so nothing passes the filter. Leave headroom for the loss of a node. Throttling applies only to pods that are already placed.

quiz.question: A service has 20 pods. Its liveness probe calls /health, which runs a query against the database. The database slows to 3 seconds per query and all 20 pods are restarted within a minute, making things worse. Which change addresses the cause?
options: Raise the liveness failure threshold and timeout so that restarts begin much later under load, which gives the database time to recover.
Keep liveness local to the process, and let readiness absorb the slow database.
Add more replicas so that some of the pods always survive each wave of restarts and keep serving.
Raise the CPU limit and memory request so the probe handler gets more resources and answers faster.
quiz.explanation: A dependency check in liveness turns a shared slowdown into a simultaneous restart of every pod. Liveness should only say whether this process is stuck. A higher threshold or more pods only delays or dilutes the same failure.
